call_notes.text: If you can't speak, call 999 and listen to the operator. If you are on a mobile and get asked, press 55 and the call goes to the police. Pressing 55 does not let the police track where you are.

If you are deaf or can't use a phone, register with the emergency text service: text REGISTER to 999 while you are safe. You get a text back that says what to do next, and after that you can text in an emergency.
NHS 111 is online for people aged 5 and over. For a child under 5, call 111.

alerts.text: Emergency Alerts come to your phone for a life-threatening emergency such as wildfire, severe flooding or an extreme storm. The phone makes a loud siren-like sound even on silent, vibrates, and may read the alert out. This lasts about 10 seconds.
They go by your current location, not where you live or work. You don't need location services on, and the government does not need your number.

Only the emergency services and government bodies that deal with emergencies can send them. An alert carries a phone number or a GOV.UK link. The service never e-mails you or asks for personal details, so treat an e-mail about it as a scam.
An alert does not replace local news, radio or television. Without a compatible phone, the emergency services have other ways to warn you.
For weather warnings, the Met Office website has the latest warnings and e-mail alerts. GOV.UK shows current flood warnings and the flood risk for the next 5 days.

first_steps.text: Stop what you're doing when an alert comes and follow its instructions. Don't read it while driving: find a safe, legal place to stop first.
Get out, stay out and call 999 if there is a fire. Don't tackle it yourself.
Be ready for 3 days: keep water, a torch with spare batteries, a battery or wind-up FM radio and a power bank. Write the frequencies of your radio stations on paper. Torches are safer than candles.
Write down the number to report a power cut. You may lose internet and some mobile signal.

hazards.text: The Be Ready site covers cold weather, snow and ice, droughts, fires in the home, flooding, hot weather and heatwaves, power cuts, storms, water supply failures, phone and broadband outages, infectious disease and terrorism, among others.
Power cuts are mostly short and local, but wider ones lasting several days can happen. Gas boilers, ovens and home internet stop without power, and your mains water may be affected.
